newsitem.title: USA: Ballooning Sept trade gap seen hurting U.S. Q3 GDP.
newsitem.headline: Ballooning Sept trade gap seen hurting U.S. Q3 GDP.

text.p: The U.S. international trade deficit unexpectedly ballooned 10.1 percent to a whopping $11.34 billion in September, prompting experts to slash forecasts for third-quarter Gross Domestic Product growth.
"It would suggest that we're going to revise down a bit on real GDP," said William Griggs, managing director of Griggs and Santow Inc.
"We had already revised down to 2.0 percent for the third quarter, and we'll probably take it under 2.0 (percent) now to 1.8 to 1.9," he added.
Economists polled by Reuters, on average, had expected the September trade gap to narrow to $9.5 billion.
The August shortfall, however, was revised lower to $10.30 billion from an originally reported $10.83 billion.
This revision somewhat lessened the negative impact of the surprising increase in September's deficit.
"Some of that is offset by the downward revision for August, but still it's going to leave you with some downward revision for GDP," Griggs said.
Total U.S. exports fell 1.4 percent to $68.79 billion in September.
On the other half of the ledger, imports rose 0.1 percent in September to $80.13 billion.

The U.S. trade deficit with the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries jumped 27.8 percent in September to $2.2 billion, the highest since November 1990. The price of imported crude oil rose to an average $20.02 a barrel, the highest since $22.98 in January 1991.
Experts were careful not to exaggerate the impact of higher crude oil and petroleum product imports because it reflected partly the pick-up in prices.

"Some of it is oil prices that jumped quite a bit and resulted in a sizable increase in petroleum imports just from the price part in addition to the volume," said Carol Stone, a senior economist at Nomura Securities International. The price component does not effect real growth, she added.
As for the impact of the trade figures on the U.S. currency, analysts adopted a cautious tone.

"The dollar is a bit weaker here and a lot of players may say in order to get this trade gap lower we need a weaker currency," said William Sullivan, director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
The trade gap has now averaged near $11 billion for three consecutive months, which Sullivan labelled a significant development.
The dollar could face some downward pressure in currency markets as a result, which may also translate into a slight negative for U.S. Treasuries, he added.
